title: Women who kept the homes
hookLine: while men rode, women farmed, hid, fed and taught

lines: EVERY RIDER CAME FROM A HOME.
cards: A knock at a farmhouse door after dark. Two riders, exhausted, horses blown. The man of the house is away with a band of his own.
The woman who opens the door has children asleep inside and soldiers searching the district. She has seconds to decide. The stories of this century follow the riders.
But every rider came from a home, and somebody kept it standing while he was gone. Today: women who kept the homes.

teach.h: THEY FARMED, HID, FED AND TAUGHT.
teach.b: Tradition remembers a long list. They farmed: with the men riding, the fields still had to be plowed, watered, harvested, and the grain hidden from tax collectors and raiders.

They hid people: riders sheltered in village houses, in grain stores, behind a wall of fodder, with a woman at the door answering questions calmly. They fed: the grain that reached the camps came from somebody's kitchen.
And they taught. Tradition says that with gurdwaras watched or seized, the prayers and the Gurmukhi letters passed from mothers to children at home, by heart.
That's one way a scripture survives persecution: at kitchen tables. Set that beside the Guru Granth Sahib.

teach.h: GURU NANAK: FROM HER, KINGS ARE BORN.
teach.b: Guru Nanak, in a passage Sikhs return to, asks why anyone would speak ill of woman, from whom kings are born. That's in paraphrase.
He describes life itself as running through women: we're born of them, bound to them, and the world goes on through them.
And Sikh tradition says the Khalsa gave women their own name, Kaur, alongside the men's Singh, with the same initiation and the same standing before the Guru.

Not long ago you met the mothers in the governor's prison who kept faith. The women who kept the homes had a quieter courage, spread over years of answering the door. The chronicles followed the riders.
But the riders had somewhere to come back to, because she held it together.

how: Sikh women take the name Kaur at initiation and share the same standing in the sangat; at home, families teach children the daily prayers and Gurmukhi, and Sikh talks honor the women who kept households through the persecutions.

games.q: you open your door after dark. two exhausted riders, soldiers searching the district, your children asleep inside. what do you do?
o: send them away to protect the children.
hide them, and answer the soldiers calmly.
games.why: tradition tells of riders sheltered in village houses, in grain stores and behind fodder, with a woman at the door.

practice: Bring to mind a woman who kept things running while the spotlight was elsewhere: a mother, grandmother, aunt, teacher, neighbor.

Picture her at the ordinary work, the meal, the bills, the door opened at the wrong hour, and stay with her face, noticing how much rested on her. If you pray, let each breath out be a quiet Waheguru for her.

wordCard.voice: Kaur, the name the Khalsa gave women alongside the men's Singh. While the riders were away, these women farmed, hid them, fed the camps and taught the children the prayers. Today's word.

orig.note: Gurmukhi for Kaur, the name women take in the Khalsa.

carryVoice: Your line: she held it together. Every rider came from a home. Eight hundred eighty-four days, and counting.
